theme: Burnt, grain, and peace offerings, substitution and fellowship
readingInstruction: Read Leviticus 1:1-3:17. A new book begins, and it starts with sacrifice. These chapters can feel strange and bloody, so read them as a guide to the way God teaches. Each offering has its own meaning, and you can learn to see it.
settingTheScene: Leviticus picks up exactly where Exodus ends. God speaks to Moses “from the tent of meeting,” since Moses could not enter it in Exodus 40. The book is mostly a manual for priests and people on how to live near a holy God. It is the central book of the Pentateuch, and its theme is holiness. It begins with the sacrifices, because without a way to deal with sin, no one could survive in God’s presence. Today’s reading covers three of the five main offerings: the burnt offering, the grain offering, and the peace offering.
observation: The burnt offering is a male without blemish. The worshiper lays his hand on its head, “and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him” (1:3-4).
The whole animal is burned on the altar, “a pleasing aroma to the LORD” (1:9).
The offering can be a bull, a sheep or goat, or a bird, depending on what the worshiper can afford (1:3, 10, 14).
The grain offering is of fine flour with oil and frankincense, and it is to be seasoned with salt but not leaven or honey (2:1-13).
Part of the grain offering is burned as a “memorial portion,” and the rest is for the priests (2:2-3).
The peace offering is shared. Part is burned, part goes to the priest, and the worshiper eats the rest (3:1-17; see 7:11-18).
Throughout, the fat and the blood belong to the LORD: “It is a statute forever throughout your generations, in all your dwelling places, that you eat neither fat nor blood” (3:17).
The phrase “a pleasing aroma to the LORD” appears repeatedly (1:9, 13, 17; 2:2, 9; 3:5, 16).
interpretation:
The three offerings you read today teach three different things about the relationship between God and his people.

The burnt offering is about atonement and total dedication. The whole animal goes up in smoke. The worshiper lays his hand on its head, and the animal dies in his place. The word “atonement” means a covering or a ransom. The sinner has forfeited his life, and the animal’s life is accepted instead. Because the whole animal is burned, it also pictures total surrender to God, a life given entirely to him.

The grain offering is a gift of thanks. It does not involve blood. It is an offering of the fruit of the worshiper’s work, flour and oil, given back to the God who provided it. It is a reminder that atonement is not the only thing in the worship of Israel. There is also gratitude.

The peace offering is the happiest of the three, and it is about fellowship. The worshiper eats part of the sacrifice, in the presence of God, with the priest and often with family and friends. After atonement and thanks, here is a meal. It is a picture of what the whole system is for: peace between God and people, shared at a table.

Notice three details that run through the chapters. First, the offering is costly. Whatever you bring must be without blemish. Second, it is accessible. A poor person could bring a bird, a handful of flour, or a dove. No one was shut out for lack of means. Third, the blood and fat belong to God, because “the life of the flesh is in the blood” (17:11), a verse you will read soon and the anchor of this unit.

The repeated phrase “a pleasing aroma” is not about smell. It means that God accepts the offering. The sacrifice is not a bribe to a hungry god. It is a way for sinners to come to a holy God and be received.
connection: Paul says that Christ “gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God” (Ephesians 5:2). He is the burnt offering, giving himself entirely. He is also our peace offering: he “is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14), and in the Lord’s Supper we eat at his table. Paul says that Christians offer their bodies “as a living sacrifice” (Romans 12:1). Hebrews 13:15-16 speaks of a “sacrifice of praise” and sharing what we have.
application:
Spend a few minutes thanking God for the gift of Christ, the one who was the perfect, complete, and accepted offering.

Ask whether you have held anything back from God. Name it and offer it to him.

The next time you take part in the Lord’s Supper, remember that it is a fellowship meal at the table of the one who made peace.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the perfect sacrifice in Jesus.
Give thanks for the atonement, the gratitude, and the peace it brings.
Offer him your life in your own words.
